title: Incentives and disincentives

draft.title: Incentives and disincentives
card: something that makes an action more rewarding or cheaper, so people and businesses are more likely to choose it.
something that makes an action less rewarding or dearer, so people and businesses are less likely to choose it.
Subsidies and rebates are incentives. A subsidy is a payment from government to a producer. A rebate gives a buyer back part of the cost. Both lower the cost of an action.
Taxes raise the cost of an action, so they are disincentives. Regulations are rules that can require or ban actions, and they can also change what is cheap or dear to choose.
draft.remember: Incentives make a choice cheaper or more rewarding. Disincentives make it dearer.

a.q: The government gives households a rebate on part of the cost of installing solar panels. What is the likely effect?
opts: It lowers the cost, so more households may install panels
It raises the cost, so fewer households may install panels
It bans panels, so households must choose another option
It changes nothing, because rebates do not affect cost
a.why: A rebate gives back part of the cost, so installing panels becomes cheaper and more households may choose it. It does not raise the cost, which is what a tax would do.
a.clue: Does a rebate make the action cheaper or dearer for the buyer?

b.q: Victoria puts a higher tax on a sugary drink, and the price rises. Which describes the tax and its likely effect on a café owner, Mia, who sells the drink?
opts: A disincentive, so Mia may choose to stock less of it
An incentive, so Mia may choose to stock more of it
A disincentive, so Mia must stop selling it
An incentive, because government collects the money
b.why: The tax makes the drink dearer to sell and buy, so it is a disincentive and Mia may stock less. It does not force her to stop, because a tax changes the cost and she still chooses. Government collecting the money does not make it an incentive.
b.clue: Does the tax make selling the drink cheaper or dearer?

a.best: It lowers the cost, so more households may install panels

b.best: A disincentive, so Mia may choose to stock less of it

problems.detail: The scenario has Victoria putting a 'higher tax' on a sugary drink. Australia has no sugary drink tax, and a state tax on goods like this would be an excise, which only the Commonwealth may levy. Students could come away thinking states can tax goods this way. Make it a federal or clearly hypothetical government.

check.summary: The card and both answers are sound. Question b wrongly suggests Victoria could put a tax on sugary drinks; that power belongs to the federal government, so change it to the Australian Government or make the scenario clearly hypothetical.
